newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers call for moratorium on U.S. executions.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers call for moratorium on U.S. executions.

text.p: The American Bar Association, citing an erosion of legal rights of death row inmates, on Monday urged an immediate halt to executions in the United States until the judicial process was overhauled.

The lawyers, who called the appeals process in capital cases "seriously flawed," said the death penalty unfairly discriminated against minorities. The ABA also demanded a halt to executions of the mentally retarded and people under 18 years old.
"If we do not stand for the insurance of basic rights, who will?" asked former U.S. Attorney General Benjamin Civiletti, now in private practice in Washington, D.C.
The United States is the only Western democracy that retains capital punishment, putting it in a league with countries such as China, Iraq, Iran and Russia.
All but 11 U.S. states have the death penalty and more than 350 people have been executed in the United States since capital punishment was reinstated by the Supreme Court in 1972.

The ABA's 19-page resolution, passed 280-119 by its policy making House of Delegates at a mid-year conference in San Antonio, reflects increased concerns that Congress and the states have limited death row appeals, the attorneys said.

"In case after case, decisions about who will die and who will live turn not on the nature of the offence the defendant is charged with committing, but rather on the nature of the legal representation the defendant receives," the resolution said.
The resolution was opposed by the U.S. Department of Justice, which said the current appeals process adequately protected the rights of death row inmates.
"This resolution would have us stop seeking death penalty cases," Jamie Gorelick, assistant U.S. attorney, told reporters.

Despite perceptions that most death row appeals are based on frivolous technicalities, four in 10 death penalty sentences appealed to federal courts on constitutional grounds are ultimately reversed, Civiletti said.
Attorneys supporting the ABA resolution said that percentage would be higher if death row inmates were assured adequate legal representation from the start.
Estelle Rogers, an ABA delegate who called for a halt to the executions, said the right to appeal on constitutional grounds "is all but eviscerated" by federal and state funding cuts.
Congress in 1996 limited federal appeals and erased federal funding of death row appeals. Several states, including Texas, also have limited the appeals process to shorten stays on death row.
"We are hopeful that the local authorities will stand up and take notice," Rogers said of the resolution.

Two U.S. Supreme Court Justices on the bench when the court upheld state death penalty statutes -- Lewis Powell and Harry Blackmun -- have since said they regretted the decision to allow executions to resume, the resolution said.

Death penalty opponents hailed the ABA proposal, which would require competent legal counsel for death row inmates and allow federal courts to review state prosecutions. But proponents said a moratorium on executions was unwarranted.
"In my opinion, the American Bar Association is beating a worn out drum on this issue," said Allan Polunsky, chairman of the Texas Board of Criminal Justice.
Texas has executed 107 people since 1972, and its highest criminal court last year upheld a law expected to shorten an appeals process that averages eight years from conviction to execution.
